**Goal:** Create a communication ecosystem that lets every employee (remote or in‑office) stay informed, feel connected across functions, and avoid the “meeting fatigue” that comes with a weekly all‑hands plus endless Slack chatter. --- ## 1. Redesigning the Communication Architecture | Layer | Tool / Format | Purpose | Frequency | |-------|---------------|---------|-----------| | **Core Pulse** | *Asynchronous status board* (e.g., Notion, Confluence “Team Dashboard”) | One‑stop shop for what each team is working on, blockers, and upcoming milestones. | Updated daily by the team lead; visible to all. | | **Sync‑and‑Share** | • **Async stand‑ups** – 1‑minute video or text update (Loom/Slack thread)
• **Weekly “Team Spotlight”** – short 5‑min video or slide deck highlighting a project, challenge, or win | Keeps everyone in the loop without live meetings. The spotlight gives cross‑functional context and celebrates work. | Stand‑ups: daily; Spotlights: weekly (rotating teams). | | **Cross‑Functional Context** | • **Monthly “Product & Ops Deep‑Dive”** – 30‑min recorded session + Q&A thread
• **Quarterly “Innovation Showcase”** – 45‑min live or pre‑recorded, followed by a Slack channel for discussion | Provides depth on how different functions contribute to the same goal. Keeps people informed without a weekly all‑hands. | Deep‑Dive: monthly; Showcase: quarterly. | | **Feedback & Collaboration** | • **Slack “Context Channels”** – one per product line or major initiative
• **Shared Docs** (Google Drive/Notion) for meeting minutes, decisions, and action items | Enables real‑time collaboration while keeping context searchable. | Continuous; docs updated after each event. | | **Governance & Visibility** | • **Communication Charter** – published in the intranet
• **Quarterly “Pulse Survey”** – quick 5‑question survey on clarity, overload, and engagement | Sets expectations, tracks health, and drives continuous improvement. | Charter: launch; Pulse: quarterly. | ### Why this works * **Asynchronous core** removes the need for everyone to be online at the same time—essential in a hybrid model with varied schedules. * **Short, focused rituals** (stand‑ups, spotlights) replace long all‑hands meetings and keep people engaged without fatigue. * **Dedicated cross‑functional channels** give context that was missing before, so employees understand how their work fits into the bigger picture. --- ## 2. Rituals That Support the Architecture | Ritual | What It Looks Like | Who Owns It | Success Signal | |--------|--------------------|-------------|----------------| | **Daily Stand‑up Thread** | Each team posts a 1‑sentence status + blocker in a dedicated Slack thread; optional Loom video for complex updates. | Team Lead | 90 % of teams post within the first 15 min each day. | | **Weekly Spotlight** | A rotating “Team Spotlight” video/slide deck (5 min) shared on the company channel, highlighting progress and next steps. | Communications Lead + team owner | Viewership > 80 % of employees; 70 % positive feedback in pulse survey. | | **Monthly Deep‑Dive** | Recorded session (30 min) with product, engineering, ops, and design leaders explaining a major initiative; Q&A thread follows. | Product Ops Manager | Attendance > 60 %; actionable questions raised. | | **Quarterly Innovation Showcase** | Live or pre‑recorded showcase of new features/initiatives + open Slack channel for discussion. | Head of R&D | Participation > 70 %; at least one idea per quarter moves to backlog. | | **Context Channels** | Dedicated Slack channels per initiative; all relevant docs pinned in the channel. | Initiative Lead | Channel activity > 50 % of team members; decisions documented. | --- ## 3. Change‑Management Plan ### Phase 1 – Diagnose & Build Momentum (Weeks 1–2) 1. **Stakeholder Mapping** – Identify champions in each function. 2. **Baseline Survey** – Quick pulse survey to capture current pain points and desired communication style. 3. **Communication Charter Draft** – Outline new rituals, tools, and expectations; circulate for feedback. ### Phase 2 – Design & Pilot (Weeks 3–6) 1. **Tool Setup** – Create Notion dashboards, Slack threads, Loom integration. 2. **Pilot Teams** – Select 4 cross‑functional teams to run the full rhythm for 4 weeks. 3. **Training Sessions** – 30‑min workshops on async communication best practices and tool usage. ### Phase 3 – Scale & Iterate (Weeks 7–12) 1. **Company‑wide Rollout** – Launch all rituals, publish charter, and make dashboards public. 2. **Feedback Loops** – Weekly check‑ins with champions; monthly pulse survey. 3. **Metrics Dashboard** – Track participation rates, survey scores, and time spent in meetings. ### Phase 4 – Institutionalize & Optimize (Ongoing) 1. **Governance Committee** – Quarterly review of rituals, tool health, and charter adherence. 2. **Continuous Improvement** – Use data to tweak frequency or format; retire under‑used rituals. 3. **Recognition Program** – Highlight teams that exemplify effective communication. --- ## Quick Wins | Action | Impact | |--------|--------| | Replace the weekly all‑hands with a 15‑min “Company Pulse” (recorded) + optional Q&A thread | Cuts meeting fatigue by ~70 % | | Mandate a 1‑minute status update in Slack for every team | Keeps everyone informed without live meetings | | Create a shared “Product Roadmap” page visible to all | Provides cross‑functional context instantly | --- ### Final Thought By shifting from a heavy synchronous model to an **asynchronous backbone** with **purposeful, short rituals**, the company can keep hybrid employees connected, reduce meeting fatigue, and ensure that everyone sees how their work contributes to the larger mission. The phased change‑management plan keeps momentum while allowing data‑driven adjustments—so the new communication architecture becomes a living part of the organization rather than another set of rules.

plan_input_messages.content:
You are the Lead Agent of a Council of Experts. Your job is to DECOMPOSE the user's question and DISPATCH precise sub-questions to the right industry specialists.

Available specialists:

- "healthcare": Llama3-Med42-8B clinical fine-tune. Strong on clinical reasoning, medical   evidence, standards of care, patient safety, healthcare operations, regulatory pathways for   therapeutics and devices, healthcare workforce.
- "legal": Saul-7B-Instruct-v1 legal fine-tune. Strong on US, UK, Canadian, and Australian   statutory and case-law frameworks, regulatory compliance, contracts, corporate law,   jurisdictional distinctions.
- "finance": Qwen-Open-Finance-R-8B finance fine-tune. Strong on unit economics, valuation   frameworks, capital structure, risk modeling, banking and insurance, financial regulation.

Approach the routing in three steps. Show your reasoning briefly (one short paragraph total across all three steps), then output the JSON.

STEP 1 — STEP BACK. State in one sentence what the user is really trying to figure out, abstracting away from the specific framing of their question.

STEP 2 — DECOMPOSE. Identify the specific analyses needed to answer the core question, and which specialist owns each. If a question doesn't require any specialist (e.g. organizing a closet), skip to the empty-routes output.

STEP 2.5 — RECENCY CHECK. Decide whether answering this question depends on recent guidance, rates, rulings, prices, regulations, or evidence that may post-date the specialists' training cutoffs. Examples that trigger recency disclosure: drug pricing or rebates, recent FDA decisions or labeling changes, evolving treatment guidelines, recent regulatory rulings, court decisions, statute amendments, current rate environments, recent agency enforcement guidance. If yes, set "requires_recency_disclosure": true and write a brief "recency_notes" string naming WHAT specifically may be stale (e.g. "GLP-1 evidence post-2024 and recent EEOC/ADA guidance"). If the question is robustly answerable from durable, non-time-sensitive foundations, set it to false.

STEP 3 — DISPATCH. For each routed specialist, write a SELF-CONTAINED sub-question that asks ONLY for their domain's contribution. Each sub-question must:

  - Include enough scenario context to be answered without the original user question (the     specialist will not see the original).
  - Focus narrowly on the specialist's domain. DO NOT ask for cross-domain analysis. DO NOT     write phrasings like "across clinical, legal, and financial dimensions" — that framing is     what causes specialists to bleed across lanes.
  - Be specific and answerable, not a topic or theme.
  - End with a clear question or directive ("What is the v1 clinical-safety design?",     "Walk through the actuarial reserve calculation", "What does the FDA SaMD pathway look like     for this device class?", etc.).

After your brief reasoning, output STRICT JSON in EXACTLY this shape, as the LAST content of your response (no markdown fence, no trailing prose):

{
  "core_question": "the abstracted core decision or analysis",
  "rationale": "1-2 sentences on why these specialists are needed",
  "routes": ["healthcare", "legal", "finance"],
  "sub_questions": {
    "healthcare": "self-contained question for the healthcare seat",
    "legal": "self-contained question for the legal seat",
    "finance": "self-contained question for the finance seat"
  },
  "requires_recency_disclosure": true,
  "recency_notes": "brief description of what may be stale (or empty string if false)"
}

Rules:
- "routes" must be a subset of {"healthcare", "legal", "finance"}.
- "sub_questions" must contain exactly one entry per element of "routes" (and no extras).
- If "routes" is empty, "sub_questions" must be {}.
- "requires_recency_disclosure" must always be present (true or false).
- "recency_notes" must be a string; empty when requires_recency_disclosure is false.
